text_fidelity_a:
CyclingDeal Upright Bike Stand - Premium Quality Vertical & Horizontal Adjustable Bicycle Floor Parking Rack - Safe & Secure for Storing MTB Road Bikes in Garage or Home - for Wheels Sizes up to 29” This CyclingDeal Upright Bike Stand gets the job done of holding my Cannondale mountain bike in place. My garage space is limited and I do not use the bike much, so I prefer the vertical configuration. If you use your bike frequently, it is easier to use the vertical configuration as getting it into the vertical position involves grabbing a dirty tire. The way this keeps the top wheel straight is better than another bike stand that uses a Velcro strap. The bike seems stable, but if I try to push it over I will be able to. I would not consider this kid-friendly in the vertical position.

This distributes the wheel weight well against three round points. Another bike stand I reviewed had the wheel rest against a thin metal bar that looked damaging to the tire.

You have to figure out how to assemble this yourself as there are no assembly instructions, just a parts diagram. They should have included instructions for the wheel rollers. The bottom wheel contact points can be adjusted into six available locations based on the wheel size. Find the correct size before tightening the screws. I did have to adjust the default center location. Adjusting these involves using two Allen wrenches. An improvement would be if there was a place to store the Allen wrenches attached to the product rather than have them mixed in a drawer of assorted Allen wrenches. I will tape the wrenches to the bottom.

The product box was damaged causing a bolt to fall out somewhere along the way. Their customer support team promptly mailed me the missing bolt.

Some of the other reviews on this product page are for a different bike stand. It looks like they swapped products after gathering reviews for the other bike stand. The current price is $70
text_fidelity_b: CyclingDeal Upright Bike Stand - Premium Quality Vertical & Horizontal Adjustable Bicycle Floor Parking Rack - Safe & Secure for Storing MTB Road Bikes in Garage or Home - for Wheels Sizes up to 29”

text_fidelity_a:
Champion Eclipse Graphite Complete Pickleball Set | Includes 3.0 Portable Net System + 4 Graphite Pickleball Paddles + 4 Outdoor Pickleballs + Pickleball Duffel Bag + USAPA Rulebook After weeks of bad weather and then surgery (and recovery) and then more bad weather, we finally had a day we could get out with this Champion Eclipse Graphite Complete Pickleball Set and give it a try. We did end up trying the paddles separate from the net (long story), but find both parts of this set really good and when we do get the chance to actual use the paddles with the net, it’ll be great. For what my wife and I consider a “beginner” and/or at home set, this is a really nice offering.

First, the “tools.” This set includes a bag (for these items), Rulebook, 4 paddles, 4 balls. All beginner level, if you get into pickle ball you’ll likely find yourself looking to upgrade, but for the backyard, for beginners, for kids or adults getting into this fast growing sport, this Champion Eclipse Graphite Complete Pickleball Set will get you off on the right foot. My wife and I are technically beginners, but we have played (not a lot), but we already do prefer longer paddles - yet we found these were good for practice. The weight is not bad, and overall they worked great. For adults or kids, they should work fine. The balls work. We play outdoors and they were fine for us. We actually got this set (primarily) for the net. The community where we live has 2 tennis courts, but also a lot of people who play tennis (most communities we’ve lived in no one does). So we wanted to have something we could take to a local park or parking lot and be able to play (we will return to club play when this Covid stuff... gets better). But we’ve used these balls and paddle on the tennis courts and they worked fine. The bag for the paddle and balls works well. It’s not top of the line, but it works fine and we’ll keep these in it for a quick grab and go.

The big plus for us was the rule book. Again, we’re only starting out and played some club stuff just before Covid. This is letting us get up to speed ahead of getting back to thing. So thrilled that was included.

The Net: this was what we really got the Champion Eclipse Graphite Complete Pickleball Set for. Again, our tennis courts can fill up when the weather allows and we were not getting any time. So we thought let’s try it. We come away very impressed. The bag it comes in is solid, well made, and while the net is slightly heavy, to us it means the materials are substantial, but not so heavy a lot of people would have an issue. We didn’t weight it, but my wife and I are guessing around 15 - 20 lbs. It did take some time to set up the first time. Working through the steps and matching the pieces - it ended up being really easy, but everything is slow going that first time. I think substantial is the best word here. We have tried a few volleyball and badminton nets and came away underwhelmed or sort of happy. This net is very good. The pieces are metal, well marked, and well designed. We set it up at the park where there was shade (our hot weather state has been off the charts hot), and got it together in less than 10 minutes - that was with undoing things for the first time, such as wrapping. Note; we kept the long plastic bags the longer pieces come in, in tact in order to store them back in each, to keep them from banging around in the bag. All the pieces of the set seem well designed and made. I would say one person could set it up easily. It also seems like, as long as you take care of it, it’ll last. There are black rubber ends to things TIP: keep them and put them back on to protect the pieces in storage.

In the end my wife and I are thrilled - not only to finally get to start using things - but with both the paddle/bag/ball/rules portion of the Champion Eclipse Graphite Complete Pickleball Set and the net part. together or separate, you’ll find a nice beginner and/or family set for a lot of fun. Our use will be varied, but we are happy to have this Champion Eclipse Graphite Complete Pickleball Set.
text_fidelity_b: Champion Eclipse Graphite Complete Pickleball Set | Includes 3.0 Portable Net System + 4 Graphite Pickleball Paddles + 4 Outdoor Pickleballs + Pickleball Duffel Bag + USAPA Rulebook

text_fidelity_a: WSTOO Bicycle seat Waterproof PU leather Mountain bike saddle high elasticity soft uni-sex cycling seat cushion-Ergonomic No nose cushions I was using a Schwinn No Nose seat which was keeping pressure off my perineum, but was a bit hard and somewhat slippery. I used the rails that came with my Schwinn saddle and they are compatible. To install this seat you must remove your old seat from the rails and LOWER the seat post. This is more work than just putting a new seat on the post as you might normally when replacing a bike seat, but not difficult to do. I find this seat is softer, has a spring like feel as you go over bumps and also has a degree of control that my other seat did not have. I don't feel as if I'm slipping off the seat as I did with the Schwinn no nose seat. I am putting less pressure on my handlebars as well which is welcome as my hands tend to get pins and needles after a while. I wrapped some fabric around the area of contact. You can move the seat a little on the rails to set it forward more. Overall an improvement from other seats for men who are looking to protect their perineum area. Maybe not the ultimate seat but a step in the right direction!

Tungsten putty is important to get your car to maximum weight. I keep the unassembled car weighted at 4.9 ounces. I drill a shallow 1/4 hole under the car and pack in the tungsten putty to make up the last bit of weight. That way on race day you can make small weight adjustments without trashing your car. The fastest car is the heaviest.

I've been getting tungsten putty from the large online derby suppliers. I figured I'd save money in shipping, use Amazon prime, and try a new product. This putty is less dense than the putty I've worked with in the past. It seems to have more sticky binder and less tungsten powder than what I've used in the past. I ordered 3 units. ELITEWHEELS Carbon Wheelset 700c Disc Brake ：UD Matte Carbon Fiber Road Bicycle Wheels 38/45/50/60/88mm Tubeless Clincher Pros: Cheap and light and are proving to be fairly durable. They're holding up to a 250lb rider on gravel and city streets. Went 20mm thru/ QR for my odd bike. They look super cool and have that neat carbon sound woo sound while riding. I saved 1 pound per wheel over the stock wheels on my Fuji Tread. Bearings seem smooth. The free hub is super loud! Louder than my Hope hubs on my MTB. It usually takes a few back pedals for pedestrians to quickly move out of my way.

Cons: You're going to fight like hell to get TL 5000gp's on these but can. Emailing these people sucks, language barrier big time as to be expected. They will work with you though to correct mistakes. I requested 6 bolt hubs they had it listed that way on the final form. They shipped with centerlock hubs. They next day aired 6 bolt adaptors for me so I could make my bikepacking trip but still not what I wanted originally. The freehub need grease I took it apart before install and one of the pawls was jammed in and needed a bit of grease and fitting to get it working.

Would buy them again. Got over 600 miles on them since purchase. Decent wheel for the price. Definitely transformed the feel of the bike.

Edit: After a year of riding 1000k+ still going great. I ran over a 2x4 at 25mph on accident while following a buddy to close. He swerved I didn't, rims still spin true and smooth. Did 40 miles of some chunker gravel with the bike fully loaded still seems unphased. I got 3 flats again no issues with the wheels other than how difficult it is to stretch the Conti's on. The bike just glides along, very happy overall with the wheels.

text_fidelity_a:
Stansport Aluminum Tent Peg, 9-Inch These stakes are well-constructed and can be pounded into reasonably hard soil without damage. I haven't destroyed any yet, but I do try to be careful when I'm pounding them into rocky ground. (A small, 8-ounce hammer works well. Larger hammers increase the likelihood of bending or breaking your stakes). The round cross section doesn't have the holding power of some of the flatter stake designs, so they don't hold as well in wind, in my experience. They're longer than most other after-market tent stakes, though (9 inches vs the more common 7-inches), which helps compensate. I like to have a few of these in my stake bag for places that the y-shaped stakes can't penetrate.

Some users have complained that they can't get their tent guylines through the holes in the silver heads. That isn't how they are intended to be used. Wrap your guyline or your anchor loop around the shaft of the stake, just below the silver head, and angle your stake to point it toward a point several feet below the center of your tent. These are fine stakes. Would like to try some of this style in a longer, 12-inch version, for larger tents that catch more wind and require stronger anchors.
text_fidelity_b: Stansport Aluminum Tent Peg, 9-Inch

Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage with | Optional LAT Pulldown & Leg Holdown Attachment | Squat and Bench Rack Combos| Super Max 810 XLT | I'm extremely pleased with the product. Assembly was straightforward and all the holes lined up! Very sturdy construction.

The attached pictures show an addition I made to turn give the rack a cable-crossover functionality. These pictures represent my Version 1.0.

All the parts can be purchased at Lowes. The rack has two perfect attachment points for the pulleys. See picture 1. This shows a threaded eye bolt and 1 1/2" fixed pulley. Two lock nuts hold it in place but it is purposely NOT tight so it has the ability to rotate. Picture 2 shows a length of zinc coated square steel tubing from Lowes. Three threaded eye bolts connect the additional cables to the center cable on the rack. Picture 3 shows me pulling on the two handles.

I think this works really well. Keep in mind, this is Version 1. One could probably cut the steel tubing length down. With the full length, it doesn't seem to hit the cage but it potentially could. NOTE: I did try this without the steel tubing and I didn't like the feel. As one completes the motion, the angle change in the cables was significant enough to notice. Your mileage may vary and you may prefer that characteristic. That tubing was the most expensive piece at about $20. Everything else is dirt cheap.

If you decide to try something like this, please be EXTREMELY careful. I am a Mechanical Engineer by education so this was something I was comfortable doing. Review the load limits of ALL the components you intend to use. For instance, the two fixed pulleys from Lowes have a safe working load of 420 pounds. I used 1/8" vinyl coated braided wire rope. Blue Hawk brand with a safe working load of 340 pounds.

Make sure ANY carabiners you use to make connections are rated for HIGH LOAD and NOT for hanging keys on your belt loop. I can't stress this enough. You do NOT want something breaking on you during full extension.

IMPORTANT: Make sure you terminate the ends of the cables correctly. Properly swaged deformable collars are likely the best approach but I used a threaded clamp for this setup. I will likely change to a swaged connection because the clamping hardware can rub against your arm during use. Also, use thimbles on the ends of both cables to protect the cable attachment points.
text_fidelity_b: Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage with | Optional LAT Pulldown & Leg Holdown Attachment | Squat and Bench Rack Combos| Super Max 810 XLT |

text_fidelity_a:
Ringside Gel Boxing MMA Hand Wraps Once in a while a product comes along that looks like it might pose a solution to a different problem than what it is actually intended for. These Ringside Gel Wraps are obviously designed to protect your hands while either working out or sparring in the ring. But I ordered them for a different unrelated purpose -- protecting my knuckles while cutting/trimming trees in our wetlands. We live in Southwest Florida where the brush grows all year around and not only grows quickly but also tries to choke out its neighbors by fighting for the available sunlight and water. That makes for tight quarters and a lot of "barked" knuckles while maneuvering tools and changing positions.

There are pros and cons to how this product is constructed:

PROS
1. They fit your hands ergonomically without limiting your flexibility. I am actually typing this review with the gloves on.
2. The gel padding on the knuckles is positioned for proper protection and provides a feeling of confidence and security.
3. There is a stretchy strap just below the knuckles that helps keep the glove in position.
4. The glove fastens around your wrist with an adjustable velcro strap.
5. There is a second strap that fastens over the first one which holds the velcro strap in place and actually provides good wrist support.
6. The gloves are breathable and machine washable.
7. Last but not least, they come in several colors: blue, grey, pink, and red.

CONS
1. Even though I am a bigger guy, I have always worn a large size in every type of glove. Be warned that these gloves run small.
2. While the overall construction is quite good, the sewing around the cut-off fingers is not uniform. The point where the gloves are
cut off (on the inside of the hand) are folded under and stitched together -- at least that was the intention. However the stitching is
"balled up" in different parts and loose strings are evident in some of the fingers. That appears to be a quality control problem.
3. I am assuming that since the gloves are too small for me that the smaller size carries over to make the fingers too tight for comfort.
Perhaps that will loosen up with wear and washing.

So overall I think that this is a great product for what it is intended, but at 65 years old I'm not the guy to punch someone with them on or
to test them out in any manner that would hurt these old bones. At my age I'm trying to protect myself, not break my hands. The manufacturer might want to take a closer look at how the fingers are sewn together, but overall this is a good looking product that should serve its purpose quite well.
text_fidelity_b: Ringside Gel Boxing MMA Hand Wraps

text_fidelity_a:
Covermates Bicycle Cover - Light Weight Polyester, Mesh Vent, Elastic Hem, Power Sports Covers-Khaki After going through 2 of those cheap plastic covers over the past few years I decided it was time to invest in a "real" cover for my bicycle which spends it's entire time outside my little apartment or where I work.

After measuring the bicycle (70L x 48H x 24W) and looking around on-line for several days, I got it narrowed down to this one from The Cover Store, and the one from Empire covers.

I went with this one because it had a fastener on the bottom to hold the cover in place (optional on the Empire cover), and I liked the tan color better than the black Empire cover.

I'm very pleased with the quality of this cover. I have my handlebars and seat set quite high, and often leave a small handlebar bag in place, and this cover still fits perfectly, covering the wheels all the way to the ground.

I'm not sure what the other folks that complained of a generic style cover got, but the one I received was obviously tailored specifically for a bicycle, and with the elastic hem fits like a glove.

I can't speak for it's durability or water resistance as I just got it, but a brief splash of water just ran off, and it seems to be made of very durable material.

I will say though, that I was so impressed that I just ordered another one.

Edit-Sept 28, 2011: I've had both covers for nearly a month now, and I'm VERY happy so far. I use my bike to commute to work, so I have a cover at both ends. Because of the elastic around the bottom, it took me a few times to figure out how to quickly and easily get the cover on and off, but here is what I've found works well for me:

First, after getting the cover on and positioned the way I wanted it, I used a magic marker to draw a fairly large triangle over the seat with the tip pointing forward and an arrow inside the triangle, also pointing forward.

Then I put a big L with a circle around it over the left handgrip and a big R with a circle around it over the right hand grip.

These 3 markers help me quickly orient and position the cover when getting ready to put it on.

What's important to realize is that the elastic around the bottom has a natural tendency to catch on things, so you simply have to learn what those things are on your particular bike and work around them.

I start by finding the triangle marker and placing that over the seat, then I get the elastic over the handlebars and down over the front wheel. Then I get the rear of the cover down over the rear wheel and around both foot pedals and the dérailleur. It takes about 2 minutes.

To get the cover off I just reverse the procedure, getting the elastic over the foot pedals and the dérailleur and then off the back wheel, then off the seat and finally over the handle bars. It takes about a minute.

This cover has plenty of room, but it's tailored in such a way as to fit nicely, and with the elastic around the bottom it's very secure. I'll report back after we get a few rains, but so far these covers are winners.

Edit (August 25, 2012): Well, I've had my two covers for a year of daily commuting to and from work, and I'm happy to report that they've met all my expectations for durability and water resistance. They still look almost new and I've had no problems with the seams leaking or showing any wear. Definitely a good investment.

Edit (September 5, 2013): Ok, it's been another year. I still use both covers for my daily commute to and from work, and they both still look really good. Only minor blemishes from being used outside all the time, but seriously, they still look very nice. Seams still all good, no wear. Elastic still like new. I've used the buckle several times during very windy weather, but probably didn't need to, because the elastic does such a good job. Yes, it still takes some time get them on and off, but I don't mind, and it's worth it to me for the excellent fit they provide. See you next year : )

Edit (January 16, 2015): Another year and a half. I really do love these covers. It's funny, people are always commenting on my "new" bicycle, and they can't believe it when I tell them it's over 15 years old. Yes, I clean and lube everything twice a year, but this bike lives outside, and it's these covers that help keep it in such good shape. A very worth while investment, and yes, the covers, although with a few stains here and there, still look practically new and function perfectly.
text_fidelity_b: Covermates Bicycle Cover - Light Weight Polyester, Mesh Vent, Elastic Hem, Power Sports Covers-Khaki

text_fidelity_a:
Hutchinson Fusion 3 Tubeless Road Tire I purchased Campy Shamal 2-way rims a couple years back. I then purchased everything needed to mount and maintain tubeless tires including Fusion 3s. I ride a '12 Specialized S-Works Roubaix and mostly do fast training rides about 3 to 4 days a week with longer rides beyond 60 miles fairly regularly. I weigh out at roughly 185 pounds.

Tubeless and ceramic bearings are somewhat in the same category these days in terms of bikers wondering if this equipment truly makes a difference. Well, I've ridden ceramic bearings in my crank and in my wheels...and YES...it makes a difference...now...I've ridden on tubeless for two riding seasons...and YES...they make a difference. Tubeless is the future...as it is in nearly every vehicle that has wheels from a riding mower to a motorcycle to a car...and mountain bikes. Why it has taken so long with road biking is understandable...change is hard...and manufacturers will go where the money is.

First, let me make this clear...putting the Fusion 3 tires on was a chore...and I mean...a CHORE. It will test your patience. Do NOT succumb to using levers as it will ruin the bead. Google tubeless tire installation for help but even then it will baffle you as to how you're going to get that tire over the rim...but...you will...and the benefits will be worth it.

Second, it takes a few rides to get the tires truly seated. Use an air compressed pump if you've got it...but...I had a "Joe Blow" floor pump that worked fine. I didn't install the sealant until after the second short ride and pump up. You will most likely lose quite a bit of air at first but as the tire seals over time...the air pressure stabilized. I do pump up my tires before every ride but it isn't out of the norm of my former clincher tires.

Third, I've ridden my fusion 3s at 90psi on the front tire and 100psi on the back. The ride is fast & super smooth. A lot of riders think super high psi is better but that is, (arguably for some), not true because at a high psi your tire is actually bumping up and down off the road which drains energy transfer over time. The benefit of running tubeless at lower psi is that the tire remains in more constant contact with the road which...over time...equals better energy transfer...and hence...speed, comfort, and endurance. Also, there is some evidence that without a tube you eliminate friction...I'm honestly not sure about that claim...even so, I can say from experience that I'm not going back to tubed tires...tubeless tires run as advertised.

Fourth, durability...I run typical roads here in Maryland over countless miles...up and down hills...less maintained side roads...and these Fusion 3s can go yet another season. The wear is normal with no unusual issues. I've NOT had one flat tire. I've NOT added more sealant since the first install...which I should've done...but...it hasn't made a difference.

Fifth, the only reservation I have is getting a flat tire but I guess it's a good thing that I'm not as use to dealing with flats like I had for my tubed tires. I have to say it has been a pleasure to not have had one flat for two seasons.

I'd like to try the ATOM version of this tire...and I think I'll get it just for comparison purposes. Not looking forward to the install and my expectation is that they will not fit my riding style, endurance expectations, and my higher weight...even so, I'm a believer in trying anything once...so...we'll see.

All in all...educate yourself but don't be afraid to go tubeless. It is change that we all seem to avoid but I'll never go back now that I've tried it out...and as the biking money goes...tubeless quality and selection will as well. ENJOY!
text_fidelity_b: Hutchinson Fusion 3 Tubeless Road Tire

Therm-a-Rest Z Lite Sol Camping and Backpacking Sleeping Pad I've backpacked with this three times now and I've had good experiences with it. That said, it has major advantages and disadvantages, so you'll need to know how this fits into your camping/backpacking situation:

Pros:
- it's insanely light
- it will keep you warm from the cold ground
- it's incapable of being punctured (it's foam) so no need to worry about mid-trip repairs regarding rips

Cons:
- it is not cushy/comfortable. If you need comfort, this is not it. It's designed for weight and heat retention, not comfort
- volume. takes up more space than an inflatable mattress pad. If you have a way to strap it outside of your back this probably isn't an issue

That is all. If you're a deep sleeper and you're doing a long, ultralight trip, this is a good option. If you need more comfort and are less concerned about weight, you may want to invest in a good inflatable mattress pad

This camp shower feels downright decadent compared to our previous habit.

For spring/summer camping it heats up to a nice warm temp in about an hour in the sun when the outside temp is in the low 70's. I wash first and use less than a gallon to get wet, wash, and rinse. Then my wife uses the rest of the water for the same, including washing/rinsing her shoulder length hair. We have two of them and occasionally she uses some of the water from the second one to finish rinsing her hair, but not always.

The shower head is a two-handed operation to pull it open for full flow or push it closed to stop the flow. We haven't had any problem with it at all. Great product.

text_fidelity_a:
Precor 9.23 Treadmill with Ground Effects Technology I decided to pick one of these up from a local dealer about two months ago because I hate going to the gym. I reasoned that if I had a treadmill in my apartment, I would have NO more excuses when it came to working out. Luckily, this has paid off for me - I've used the treadmill nearly every day since it was delivered. I really love this treadmill so far.

The Precor was more expensive than similar models, but they seem to have a better reputation when it comes to quality, reliability, customer service, and repairs when things DO go wrong.

When I was testing out treadmills at the store, the Precor definitely did feel more sturdy and well built, even though it's one of their cheaper, Chinese made models. And even though the 9.23 is made in China, I was told that replacement parts are stocked in the US (if that means anything to anyone).

I use my treadmill for walking on an incline only. The manual says that it supports users up to 550 pounds for walking only, and 350 pounds for running (which is much higher than other, cheaper models). I started using the treadmill when I was about 330 pounds, and have never had any major problems with it (I'm down 8 pounds last time I checked). The motor doesn't jerk or hesitate at all, even for someone as heavy as me.

One thing to note regarding the maximum weight: the dealer told me to add 50 pounds to the maximum if you're going to run, so I would have exceeded the 350 pound max if I had done so. This didn't bother me though as I had only planned on walking at an incline anyway.

The only minor issue I've had so far is a slight bit of belt slippage under my right foot. There isn't anything in the manual about this, but after doing some research, I figured out how to tighten the belt a bit so this wouldn't happen. The belt would also go off center as well due to it being too loose. I haven't had a problem since tightening it.

The manual talks about centering the belt using the bolt on the right side of the belt only. To tighten the belt, you just have to do equal clockwise turns on each side of the belt while the treadmill is set to around 3 MPH - maybe a quarter or eighth turn at a time making sure the belt stays centered. I was very conservative about this, testing for slippage after each small turn, and I didn't have to tighten the belt much. This was pretty easy, but Precor will have the local repair people come out if you are at all uncomfortable doing this yourself.

I also called Precor customer service about the belt slippage just to be safe, and I also wanted to see how that whole process would go. When I called, I got connected to someone in the US nearly right away. The customer service agent directed me to the local repair guy, who confirmed what I had found about tightening the belt (he didn't need to come out). The agent seemed rather knowledgable about the product, and cleared up some wrong information I got from the dealer as well. So far, I'm pretty happy with Precor customer service.

The dealer told me I'd need to lubricate the belt, but the manual for the 9.23 says you never need to do this. Customer service confirmed that the 9.23's belt does NOT need to be lubricated.

The sound of the treadmill running and my footsteps are rather loud, but nothing too annoying when you wear headphones and listen to music. If others are in the room, it might be disturbing to them though.

The treadmill has a rather strong odor to it at first that DOES seem to diminish over time. The best way I can describe it is a plastic and/or electronics smell. It's not terrible, but it's not exactly lovely either.

The electronics are ultra basic - just what I wanted. You get a few programs and start, stop, incline and speed controls and that's it. I actually prefer this since I only ever use manual controls anyway, and I have other gadgets I use to do anything fancy.

The 9.23 doesn't have side rails, which is a bit uncomfortable at first, but I've gotten used to it. The next model up has rails and a few other things, but I didn't think it was worth the extra cost even though I really would prefer rails in order to steady myself. This is a minor issue that I've learned to live with.

There is a small ledge under the screen that's perfect for a Kindle or a tablet. I have a [[ASIN:B00HWMPSFQ Samsung Galaxy Tab Pro 10.1 Tablet (Black)]], and it sits securely on the ledge even at 6% incline. I listen to music and use the Kindle app to read, or I listen to Audible audiobooks, and the time flies by. I have little trouble motivating myself to walk in the mornings.

The treadmill has a built-in heart rate monitor when you grip the handles. I have found this to be practically useless though, as the reading jumps up and down way too much, and it takes way too long to get a reading. I wanted to track heart rate, so I bought the Polar H7 heart rate sensor and paired it to my phone, and I use the Polar Beat app to track heart rate, time, and calories burned. So far I'm really loving this system.

The last thing I'll mention has more to do with modern circuit breakers than the treadmill itself. When I first got the treadmill, turning it on would trip adjacent breakers if there was a certain load above maybe around 100 watts on it, like a bathroom light and fan for example. I had never heard of a device tripping a DIFFERENT circuit breaker, but apparently this is very common with treadmills.

Apparently, treadmill motors emit some type of interference that trips newer types of circuit breakers (AFCI). Luckily there is an easy fix for this - all you have to do is plug the treadmill into a [[ASIN:B0000513O4 Tripp Lite ISOBAR4ULTRA Isobar Surge Protector Metal 4 Outlet 6 feet Cord 3330 Joules]] or something similar. I've also tried the [[ASIN:B0000510R4 Tripp Lite ISOBLOK2-0 2-Outlet Isobar Premium Surge Protector 1410 Joules]] but it didn't work. I know other similar surge protectors with EFI/RFI line noise filtering have been reported to work too, but I've only tried the Tripp Lite.

Overall, I'm really glad I spent the extra money on the Precor. It feels sturdy and meets my basic needs, and I have confidence that if I do have a problem, I'll be able to get it taken care of without a ton of hassle.
text_fidelity_b: Precor 9.23 Treadmill with Ground Effects Technology

Now, having a container that’ll stay ice cold all night without peeing the bed, that can be a challenge. These are the most durable water bladders I’ve found, and after a year of being frozen and thawed every day, filled to about 85-90% with a little room left for expansion, they show absolutely no real signs of wear. They’ve gotten dirty, and I’ve had to scrub them now and then, but they are very reliable. My only issue has been the tiny nozzle on the little cap, which will occasionally pop open and cause problems. That’s easily fixed with a piece of duct tape. Considering what I put these things through, I really couldn’t imagine finding a better alternative.

It would be nice if they could make the fabric covering a smoother texture, but honestly, that’s a particularly nit-picky detail that most people using these for intended purposes, couldn’t care less about.

These things last so long, if you don’t lose them and you’re not using them in active military service, I seriously doubt you’ll need to replace them for a long time to come. I bet if I’d had one while I was in the army, I’d still be using it. They’re far tougher than the 2-quart canteens I was issued, that’s for sure.

Units fold up quite compactly.

text_fidelity_a:
VP Components VP-Vice Pedals (Pack of 2) There are some interesting patterns that you'll see if you read through the reviews. Some people recevied their pedals shrink wrapped, and they scratch the other pedal in transport. Some people get new pedals in a box, and life is wonderful because they got an awesome pedal set at an awesome price. And some people get pedals in a box that look brand new, but have blown bearings. I'm in that third group.

I bought this pair from cyclingdeal_usa, fulfilled by Amazon. I was happy to see the pedals arrive looking brand new in a box similar to the one my first Vices showed up in about five years ago. I'm a huge fan of these pedals, and the fact that I have a the titanium pins for my primary bike, and that they're now as ridiculously affordable as they are means it makes sense to put these on the other bikes in the house.

I bought these for my son's bike, and the look great, but there was a click with each stroke on the left pedal. I threw them on my bike, on the titanium pins, and there was still a click with each stroke. I changed out the bearings (I had a rebuild kit on hand) and boom, the pedals are exactly as they should be, and the click is gone.

Like some other people's reviews, my VP-Vice Pedal set showed up with blown bearings. The right pedal was fine, but the left pedal clicked out of the box, and that's the first time I've seen a pair of Vice pedals do that. I see they're currently at the best price through VP Components. I'm hopeful that means they're shipped in a new box, and that if there's any issues, I know from a past experience with them, that VP Components will make it right.

I'm rating this purchase 4*, because I love the pedals, I love VP components, and I'm very happy with the bang for the buck of getting all my bikes on Vice pedals, but I hate that I had to use my rebuild kit to get working bearings in left pedal. (Yeah, I know I could have returned them, but I wanted to get them on my son's new bike, and we were all excited to go riding.)
text_fidelity_b: VP Components VP-Vice Pedals (Pack of 2)

text_fidelity_a:
Suunto 3 Fitness Tracker Sports Watch This is a great fitness watch, but it's not that good of a smart watch. I wouldn't suggest cross shopping this with a Samsung Gear or Apple Watch, as they can do quite a bit more than this. Likewise some of the newer Garmin watches are a bit more capable, but if you're looking for a fitness watch (with some smart watch features), this is a very good option.

It sets up quickly, although the charger is more akin to what I expected from 2015 than 2018. It clips on, and it charges reasonably quickly. It has a guided setup and decent instructions that will help walk you through using the watch. I'd rely on those, as it's not the most intuitive watch. Apple and Samsung have them beat there (I haven't used a Garmin). In regards to use, I find the GPS to be quite accurate (compared to phone) and the heart rate and steps to be accurate (compared to a Fitbit). Both do well compared to my own non-scientific tests (ie the heart rate looked right and the recorded journey matched my recollection).

I would say that a Samsung, Apple (if you use iPhones), and Garmin would be more broadly recommended. This is a bit of a fitness watch for fit people (the Garmin fits the bill there), and it's not a "lifestyle accessory" or gizmo. I found the focus on fitness to be refreshing and a bit of a reminder of what I'm trying to do, but I couldn't send tunes to my earbuds or other stuff I can do with some of my other watches. I find it to be a solid tradeoff, but it may not be for you.

4 stars for being a bit niche but not being absolutely amazing at that niche.
text_fidelity_b: Suunto 3 Fitness Tracker Sports Watch

There are 10 holes/slots for the golf balls to land in with points ranging from 5 to 100. 5 of the 10 balls are white and the other 5 are yellow. text_fidelity_a:
YOUR Pillow! by SHO - Ultimate Self Inflating Travel, Camping & Festival Pillow I love camping, but it's hard to bring your bed pillow and worry about it getting dirty, along with trying to find room to fit it in with all of the other stuff you need to bring along. When you have a family, the space you have to bring stuff gets very small. This little pillow is perfect for traveling/camping. It comes in a little bag. When you unstrap it, you just open the valve. Once that happens, it puffs up and inflates to about half. This is comfortable as you can feel the foamy inside, but if you want it firmer, just blow into the valve. This allows you to blow it up to your liking. It's comfortable. I have tried folding up clothing to use as a mock pillow and it just gives you a sore neck, so this is a way better option. To put it back in the bag, just open the valve again, press all the air out and roll it up like a toothpaste tube. Then put the band around it and stick it back in the bag. It never goes in quite like it did originally, but it still fits in fine. Then you can use the string on the bag to hang it on a clip on your backpack or purse. The pattern is fun and bright, so you won't lose it anywhere, and the outside is waterproof so it can be wiped off instead of having to put it in the wash like a big pillow. I love having this and my neck will be much happier than when I slept on a balled up sweater.

*I RECEIVED THIS ITEM TO TRY AT A DISCOUNTED PRICE (IN ORDER TO LEAVE AN HONEST AND UNBIASED REVIEW) THIS DOES NOT GUARANTEE A GOOD REVIEW, SO IF I GIVE THE PRODUCT ONE, IT DESERVES IT ON IT'S OWN MERIT. ALL OF THE REVIEWS I WRITE ARE MY OWN AND I NEVER ALLOW ANYONE OR ANYTHING TO INFLUENCE THEM IN ANY WAY
